rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s promise to his people resembles the promise Muhammad makes to his people in 61:10–14.
rows.anchor: The promise given by Noah to his people in these verses is similar to that given by the Prophet Muhammad to his people in 61:10–14.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Sky” is a metonym for rain.
rows.anchor: The sky is often used as a metonym for “rain,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a desert setting, rain signifies great blessing and even the gift of life.
rows.anchor: which in a desert environment is synonymous with great blessing, even with the gift of life itself.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Midrār, translated “abundant,” describes something sent repeatedly.
rows.anchor: Abundance translates midrār, which indicates something that is sent again and again.

rows.speaker: most
rows.claim: Most commentators take midrār to indicate rain.
rows.anchor: Most interpret it as an indication of rain.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise may encompass all Divine blessings, material and spiritual, promised to disbelievers if they revere God.
rows.anchor: it can be taken as a reference to all manner of Divine Blessings, both material and spiritual, promised to the disbelievers elsewhere on the condition that they reverence God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question asks why people do not hope that God will honor and magnify them in this life, the Hereafter, or both.
rows.anchor: This verse means, “How is it that you do not hope that God will honor you and magnify you [Q, R, Z] in this life

rows.speaker: Āl, Ṭs
rows.claim: Some commentators instead understand the question as asking why people do not fear God with dignity.
rows.anchor: Some commentators read this to mean, “How is it that you do not fear God with dignity?” (Āl, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stages refer to all phases of human existence and serve as proof of God’s power.
rows.anchor: These verses allude to all stages of human existence, which are cited as proof of God’s Power

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the creation of the seven heavens one upon another, the commentary points to 67:3–4.
rows.anchor: For the creation of the seven heavens one upon another, see 67:3–4c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The moon and sun allude to the guidance God provides; 10:5 also describes them as signs that guide reckoning.
rows.anchor: The mention of the moon and the sun alludes to the means of guidance that God has provided

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 16 may begin “and that He” with verses 17 and 19, continuing the rhetorical question begun in verse 15.
rows.anchor: V. 16 could be read with “and that He” at the beginning with vv. 17 and 19, also beginning with “and that,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Like plants” can mean “as growing things.”
rows.anchor: Like plants can mean “as growing things.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase alludes to humans being created from dust, as in the likeness of Adam and Jesus described in 3:59.
rows.anchor: On the one hand, this alludes to the creation of human beings from dust, as in 3:59

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The diversity of growing things also points to all things emerging from God as one ontological Source, whose substance is within them.
rows.anchor: it alludes to the manner in which all things are thought to emerge from a single source, God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If verse 14 concerns only life’s stages, this verse extends them through death and resurrection, as in 2:28.
rows.anchor: When v. 14 is read as referring only to the stages of existence during this life, this verse would complete it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth as an open expanse recalls its description as a cradle with paths threaded through it in 20:53.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere God is described as the One Who made the earth a cradle for you, and threaded paths for you therein (20:53).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spacious paths indicate other means of guidance God has provided, like the guidance associated with sun and moon in verse 16.
rows.anchor: spacious paths indicates other means of guidance that God has provided

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Enwrapped” refers to the Prophet wrapping himself in his cloak after the first revelation.
rows.anchor: Enwrapped refers to the Prophet’s wrapping himself in his cloak after the first revelation

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: ʿAlī names al-Muzzammil among seven Quranic names for the Prophet, alongside Muhammad, Aḥmad, Ṭā Hā, Yā Sīn, al-Muddaththir, and ʿAbd Allāh.
rows.anchor: According to ʿAlī ibn AbīṬālib, thou enwrapped

rows.speaker: most
rows.claim: Most understand the name as the Prophet’s cloaking himself in awe of the new revelation.
rows.anchor: Thou enwrapped is understood by most as a reference to the Prophet’s wrapping himself in his cloak in awe of the new revelation

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: In this sūra’s context, the address may instead tell the Prophet to leave his bedding and rise for prayer, as if calling him “O thou who art sleeping.”
rows.anchor: in the context of this sūrah, it can also be seen as an injunction from God to throw off one’s bedding and stand in prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before the five daily prayers, night vigil was common for the Prophet and his small group of followers, who reportedly prayed until their feet swelled.
rows.anchor: Before the five daily prayers were revealed, night vigil was the common practice of the Prophet and his small group of followers, who would reportedly stand in prayer until their feet swelled.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The practice was eased in verse 20 and explicitly made supererogatory in 17:79.
rows.anchor: The practice was then eased in v. 20 and was made explicitly supererogatory in 17:79

rows.speaker: a famous ḥadīth
rows.claim: A famous report says that in the night’s last third God descends to the lowest heaven and calls for people to invoke, ask, or seek forgiveness so that He may respond, give, or forgive.
rows.anchor: a famous ḥadīth says, “Every night during the last third of the night, our Lord descends to the Heaven of this earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran presents night vigil as a supererogatory practice of the upright among the People of the Book and cites it in several other passages.
rows.anchor: Night vigil is also a supererogatory practice that the Quran attributes to the upright among the People of the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These are the earliest-revealed verses explicitly to enjoin Quran recitation as worship, a command repeated in other passages.
rows.anchor: These are the first verses in the chronological order of revelation to explicitly enjoin reciting the Quran as a form of worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The measured-recitation command may apply to all Muslims or specifically to the Prophet as he delivers revelation to others.
rows.anchor: The command to recite the Quran in a measured pace can be seen as an injunction for all Muslims or as one that applies specifically to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s measured recitation reflects God’s own description of how He recited revelation to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: In this way the Prophet’s manner of recitation reflects the manner that God ascribes to Himself in 25:32

rows.speaker: Umm Salamah
rows.claim: Umm Salamah reports that the Prophet recited verse by verse, pausing at each verse’s end.
rows.anchor: his wife Umm Salamah is reported to have said, “He used to divide his recitation verse by verse”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet urged his followers to adorn the Quran with their voices.
rows.anchor: The Prophet enjoined his followers to recite the Quran, saying, “Adorn the Quran with your voices”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet says that one who does not chant the Quran is not one of his followers.
rows.anchor: The Prophet enjoined his followers to recite the Quran

rows.speaker: aḥādīth
rows.claim: A report promises that fluent Quran reciters accompany the honorable, obedient angelic scribes, while those who recite with difficulty receive double reward.
rows.anchor: Whosoever recites the Quran fluently is with the honorable and obedient scribes [i.e., the angels], and whosoever recites it with difficulty shall receive a double reward

rows.speaker: aḥādīth
rows.claim: A report promises peace, mercy, angelic attendance, and God’s remembrance for a group gathered in a house of God to recite and contemplate scripture.
rows.anchor: Never does a group gather in one of the houses of God, reciting the Book of God and contemplating it, but that peace descends upon them

rows.speaker: a famous ḥadīth
rows.claim: A famous report likens the believer who recites Quran to a sweet citrus fruit and the nonreciting believer to a sweet dried date; the reciting hypocrite is fragrant but bitter, while the nonreciting hypocrite is bitter apple.
rows.anchor: Regarding the different levels of recitation, a famousḥadīth states

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: “Lengthy affairs” means daytime responsibilities that leave no time for extensive devotion.
rows.anchor: Lengthy affairs refers to the responsibilities that prevent one from having time for extensive devotions during the day (JJ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Alternatively, God grants an extensive span for worldly matters, implying that a part of the night should be devoted to prayer.
rows.anchor: or to God’s granting an extensive expanse of time for worldly matters, thus implying the responsibility to devote a part of the night to prayer (IK).

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Once believers finish their affairs, they should devote themselves to God, as in the command to exert oneself when free in 94:7.
rows.anchor: Once believers have finished with their affairs, they should devote themselves to God, as in 94:7

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Some understand remembering the Lord’s Name as reciting the basmalah at the start of Quran recitation.
rows.anchor: Some say the command remember the Name of thy Lord means to recite the basmalah (In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful), at the beginning of Quranic recitation (JJ)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Others take the command as urging remembrance of God at every moment of every day, since God’s remembrance is greater.
rows.anchor: others see it as an exhortation to remember God at every moment of every day (Aj), since the remembrance of God is surely greater (29:45).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabattal literally means to sever or cut off.
rows.anchor: Devote translates tabattal, which literally means “to sever” or “to cut off.”

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The command is interpreted as cutting oneself off from everything other than God’s remembrance.
rows.anchor: It is thus interpreted to mean cutting oneself off from everything other than the remembrance of God (Aj).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night vigil in this verse is the form of vigil commanded in verses 1–8.
rows.anchor: The form of night vigil mentioned in the first sentence relates to that enjoined in vv. 1–8

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Probably revealed about twelve months after verses 1–8, this verse removed the night vigil’s obligatory status and made it voluntary.
rows.anchor: Most likely revealed some twelve months after those verses, the present verse revoked the obligatory status of the night vigil and made it voluntary

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The group with the Prophet were Companions who copied his practice and reportedly stood until their feet swelled.
rows.anchor: A group of those who are with thee refers to the small group of Companions who emulated the Prophet’s practice at that time, standing in prayer until their feet were swollen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the first sentence, the address shifts from the Prophet alone to the Prophet and his Companions together.
rows.anchor: After the first sentence, this verse changes from addressing the Prophet in the second-person singular to addressing the Prophet and his Companions in the second-person plural.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The statement that they would not keep count means the Companions could not all fulfill the full night-vigil obligation.
rows.anchor: You will not keep count of it indicates that the Prophet’s Companions would not all be able to perform the obligation in full (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God relented by reducing the vigil requirement and letting them recite as much Quran in prayer as was easy.
rows.anchor: Therefore, He has relented unto you by lessening the requirement to stand in vigil and allowing them to recite as much of the Quran as is easy for them in prayer

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some held that those who know the Quran should still recite at least fifty or one hundred verses.
rows.anchor: According to some, those who know the Quran should still recite a minimum of fifty or one hundred verses

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Another view lowers the minimum recitation for those who know the Quran to five verses.
rows.anchor: or even just five (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night vigil is difficult for the sick, travelers, and fighters, so they need only perform what is not too taxing.
rows.anchor: For those who are sick, traveling, or fighting, performing the night vigil is difficult, so they need only perform that which is easy of it

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some infer from the mention of fighting that this verse dates from the Medinan period, since fighting began there.
rows.anchor: The mention of fighting in this verse has caused some to surmise that it is from the Madinan period, as fighting did not begin until then.

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others see the fighting as foreshadowing the trials faced by the early Muslim community.
rows.anchor: Others see it as foreshadowing the travails that the early Muslim community would face (IK).

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: “Perform the prayer” refers to the obligatory daily prayers.
rows.anchor: Perform the prayer refers to the obligatory daily prayers (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the first mention of alms (zakāh) in revelation’s chronological order.
rows.anchor: This verse contains the first mention of alms

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some interpret zakāh here as the obligatory alms.
rows.anchor: Some interpret it as a reference to the obligatory alms

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because zakāh’s specific form was not yet institutionalized, the verse may refer to charity generally.
rows.anchor: but since the specific form of zakāh was not institutionalized at this time, it may refer to charity in general.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say payment of alms was required in the Makkan period, while its detailed rules were established only in the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: Some say that the requirement to pay alms was established during the Makkan period, but that the specifics were not established until the Madinan period (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lending a goodly loan means spending effort and wealth for religion’s cause; in 5:12 and here it is linked with prayer and almsgiving.
rows.anchor: To lend unto God a goodly loan (2:245; 5:12; 57:11, 18; 64:17) indicates expending effort and wealth for the cause of religion

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Whatever good believers send ahead for themselves comprises all their good deeds in this life.
rows.anchor: Whatever good you send forth for your souls refers to all good deeds performed by believers in this life (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Spending in God’s way during life is better than what one keeps for oneself or leaves as inheritance.
rows.anchor: what one spends in the way of God in this life is better than what one keeps for oneself or leaves behind as an inheritance (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reward also alludes to the increase of good deeds in the Hereafter, as in the parable of multiplied grain in 2:261 and related verses.
rows.anchor: It also alludes to the manner in which good deeds are increased in the Hereafter, as in 2:261

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: This is the Prophet’s first call to deliver revelation and propagate the message, while 96:1–5 is regarded as his first call to prophethood.
rows.anchor: Arise and warn indicates that this is the first call to the Prophet to deliver the new revelation, to propagate the prophetic message

rows.speaker: My
rows.claim: Spiritually, the verses call all people to remove what separates them from God, arise through God, and abandon everything besides God.
rows.anchor: From a spiritual perspective, vv. 1–2 can be understood as a call to all human beings to remove what separates them from God

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The companions of the right ask about fellow believers who failed to act according to revelation and now face this predicament.
rows.anchor: The companions of the right are said to question one another about the predicament of their fellow believers who had failed to act in accord with the revelation

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase simply means they question the sinners directly.
rows.anchor: Others interpret questioning one another to simply mean“questioning,” indicating that they speak directly to the sinners (Q, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is among passages showing that, at least sometimes, people in the Garden and Fire can communicate in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: This would then be one of several passages to indicate that in the Hereafter those in the Garden and those in the Fire are, at least on occasion, able to communicate with one another

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The Reminder refers to the Quran.
rows.anchor: Here the Reminder is a reference to the Quran (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: People turn away from the Quran either by denying it or by failing to act according to it.
rows.anchor: from which people turn away either by denying it or by not acting in accord with it (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary renders qaswarah as “lion.”
rows.anchor: Lion translates qaswarah, an enigmatic word

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Other interpretations of qaswarah are hunting spears, arrows, or hunters.
rows.anchor: also interpreted to mean “hunting spears,” “arrows,” or “hunters” (Q, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Each man wants a revelation addressed directly to him, like those who ask why God does not speak to them or send them a sign.
rows.anchor: Each man wants a revelation that is addressed directly to him (Q, Ṭ), as in 2:118

rows.speaker: some of the Quraysh
rows.claim: Some Quraysh objected that, if Muhammad were truly God’s Messenger, he could give each of them a book granting exemption and protection from the Fire.
rows.anchor: It is also reported that some of the Quraysh objected by saying that, if Muhammad were truly a Messenger of God, he could bring a book that would give each of them exemption

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The emphatic particle kallā can also mean “truly” or “indeed,” a rendering that suits verse 54 better than verse 53.
rows.anchor: In both verses nay, translating the emphatic particle kallā, could also be rendered “truly” or “indeed,” an alternative that fits v. 54 better than v. 53 (Q).

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿĀmir
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads “you fear not” rather than “they fear not,” turning the phrase into a warning to the reader or listener.
rows.anchor: In the recitation of Ibn ʿĀmir, they fear not is read, “you fear not,” as a warning to the reader or listener.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The Reminder is the Quran.
rows.anchor: Reminder refers to the Quran (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation is a reminder rather than a list of demanded proofs: it reawakens knowledge of God and the covenant all humans carry in their primordial nature.
rows.anchor: Rather, as a reminder, the revelation reawakens the knowledge of God and of the covenant with Him (see 7:172c) that all human beings bear in their primordial nature (30:30).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As rendered, remembering means especially acting in accordance with God’s Word in the Quran.
rows.anchor: As rendered, this verse refers to remembering, particularly in the sense of acting in accord with the Word of God in the Quran.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may mean that whoever wills may remember God.
rows.anchor: It could also be read as referring to the remembrance of God: “So let him who will, remember Him.”

words: بَلَىٰ قَٰدِرِينَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن نُّسَوِّىَ بَنَانَهُۥ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can resurrect a person exactly as He first created him.
rows.anchor: This verse is said to mean, “We are able to create him again precisely as we created him the first time”
